sections.h: Luke 14–17: the heart of Luke's own material
sections.b: Much of what readers think of as most typical of Luke comes from these chapters, and most of it is found in no other Gospel: the advice to invite the poor, the crippled, the lame and the blind (Luke 14:12–14), the tower and the king (Luke 14:28–32), the lost coin and the father with two sons (Luke 15:8–32), the shrewd manager (Luke 16:1–8), the rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16:19–31), the slave who has only done his duty (Luke 17:7–10), the ten men cleansed and the one Samaritan who gave thanks (Luke 17:11–19), and the saying that the kingdom of God is among you (Luke 17:20–21). Scholars call this special material "L." Its themes run through the whole Gospel: God's search for the lost, joy at meals, reversal of rich and poor, the welcome of outsiders, and money as a test of the heart.

sections.h: Luke 14–16: parables at table and on the road
sections.b: Luke 14–16 holds some of the best-known parables, most found only in Luke. At a Pharisee's dinner Jesus tells of the places at table and of the great supper whose invited guests all make excuses, so that the poor, the crippled, the blind and the lame are brought in instead (Luke 14:7–24). To the crowds he gives twin parables of a builder and a king who count the cost (Luke 14:28–32). To Pharisees who grumble at his meals with sinners he tells one parable in three panels: the lost sheep, the lost coin and the father with two sons, each ending in a celebration, the last left open with the elder son outside (Luke 15). Then come the shrewd manager, praised for acting decisively in a crisis, and the rich man and Lazarus, the only parable with a named character (Luke 16). Luke sets several of these where Matthew does not, and the setting changes the point: the lost sheep is about sinners in Luke and about straying church members in Matthew 18:12–14.

common: The parable of the two sons (the prodigal son) is the most retold of all Jesus' parables.
uncommon: Some scholars think the parable of the shrewd manager praises the manager for cancelling forbidden interest, so that he acted rightly after all.

sections.h: Luke 15: joy over one who repents
sections.b: Luke 15 is the Bible's fullest picture of repentance from God's side. A shepherd searches for a lost sheep and a woman for a lost coin, and each time Jesus says there is joy in heaven "over one sinner who repents" (Luke 15:7, 10). The younger son "came back to himself," planned a confession ("Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight") and went home, but his father ran to him before he could finish (Luke 15:17–21). Readers debate whether the son's turning was true repentance or a plan to eat; either way, the welcome is the father's gift. Luke frames all three stories as Jesus' answer to critics of his meals with "tax collectors and sinners" (Luke 15:1–2). Luke 17:3–4 adds that disciples must forgive a brother who repents, even seven times a day.

common: The parable of the prodigal son is commonly read as the picture of a sinner's conversion.
uncommon: Amy-Jill Levine argues that the lost sheep and coin cannot repent, so the parables are first about God's joy in finding, not about repentance.

sections.h: Luke 15 and 17: the father's welcome and forgiveness seven times a day
sections.b: The father in Luke 15 forgives before the son finishes his confession: he runs, embraces him, gives him the best robe, a ring and sandals, and throws a feast (Luke 15:20–24). His words to both sons, "was dead ... alive ... lost ... found," set the tone of Luke's Gospel of mercy. In Luke 17:3–4 Jesus asks the same of disciples: rebuke a brother who sins, forgive him if he repents, and keep forgiving even seven times in one day, Luke's equivalent of Matthew's "seventy-seven times" (Matthew 18:21–22).

sections.h: Luke 14 and 16: possessions, the manager and the rich man
sections.b: Luke presses harder on wealth than any other Gospel. "None of you can be a disciple of mine if he does not say goodbye to all his possessions" (Luke 14:33). The parable of the shrewd manager teaches disciples to use "the wealth of dishonesty" to make friends who will welcome them into the everlasting tents, to be faithful with money so that God can trust them with true riches, and to remember that no one can serve both God and wealth (Luke 16:1–13). The Pharisees, "fond of money," sneer (Luke 16:14), a charge that is Luke's polemic rather than a fair picture of the movement. The rich man who dressed in purple and made merry every day, while Lazarus lay at his gate, ends in torment; his sin is not named except that he did not listen to Moses and the Prophets, who command care for the poor (Luke 16:19–31; Deuteronomy 15:7–11). John Wesley preached on Luke 16:9 his sermon "The Use of Money": gain all you can, save all you can, give all you can.

common: "Mammon" (Luke 16:9, 11, 13) is the Aramaic word for wealth, not the name of a demon.
uncommon: Some readers think the rich man of Luke 16 hints at the high-priestly family of Annas, which had five sons.

sections.h: Luke 14 and 16: the poor at the table and at the gate
sections.b: Jesus tells a Pharisee host to invite "people who are poor, crippled, lame or blind," who cannot repay, and the parable of the great supper fills the host's house with the same four groups (Luke 14:13, 21). The list matches those whom the Law kept from priestly service (Leviticus 21:18) and whom a Qumran rule kept from Israel's end-time assembly. The poor man Lazarus, the only invented character in Jesus' parables to be given a name, lies at a rich man's gate longing for what falls from his table, with dogs licking his sores; at death he is carried to Abraham's embrace (Luke 16:20–22). His name, from Eleazar, means "God has helped." In medieval Europe he became the patron of the sick poor, which gave English "lazar" and "lazaretto."
sections.refs: Luke 14:12–14; Luke 14:21; Luke 16:19–25; Leviticus 21:17–23; Deuteronomy 15:11; Luke 4:18; Luke 6:20

sections.h: Luke 16: Hades in the parable of the rich man and Lazarus
sections.b: Luke 16:19–31 is the New Testament's most detailed picture of the dead before the judgment. Lazarus is carried by angels to "Abraham's embrace," the place of honor at a feast; the rich man is "in Hades," in torment and flame, able to see Abraham far off but separated by "a huge gulf" that no one can cross. The picture resembles 1 Enoch 22, where the spirits of the righteous and of sinners are kept in separate places until the great judgment. Hades here is not Gehenna, the final punishment after the resurrection (Luke 12:5). Christians disagree whether the parable describes the actual state of the dead or uses familiar pictures to make a point about this life; Catholic, Orthodox, Reformed, Baptist, Adventist and Jehovah's Witness views are set out in the card on Luke 16.
sections.refs: Luke 16:22–31; 1 Enoch 22:1–14; Luke 12:5; Luke 23:43; Acts 2:27, 31; Revelation 20:13–14

common: Many Christians take Luke 16 as proof that the dead are conscious before the resurrection.
uncommon: Seventh-day Adventists and Jehovah's Witnesses read Luke 16:19–31 as a parable that teaches nothing about the state of the dead.

sections.h: Luke 16: the fixed gulf and prayer for the dead
sections.b: Abraham tells the rich man that "a huge gulf has been set firm" between the righteous and the wicked dead (Luke 16:26). Protestant confessions cite the parable to show that a person's state is fixed at death, with no purgatory (Westminster Confession 32.1 lists Luke 16:23–24). Catholic teaching replies that the gulf separates the saved from the lost, while purgatory is a purification of the saved, and it cites the parable for the particular judgment and for "Abraham's bosom," where the righteous before Christ awaited him (Catechism 633, 1021). The Latin funeral antiphon prays that the dead may rest "with Lazarus, who once was poor."

sections.h: Luke 14–15: the supper of the kingdom
sections.b: A guest at a Pharisee's table says, "How blessed is whoever eats bread in the kingdom of God!" (Luke 14:15). Jesus answers with the parable of the great supper: those first invited make excuses, and the host fills his house with the poor and disabled and with people from the country roads, so that "not one of those invited men will taste my supper" (Luke 14:16–24). The plural "I tell you" turns the story on the listeners. The father's feast for the lost son, with the fattened calf, music and dancing, is another picture of the joyful meal of the kingdom, and the elder son is left outside deciding whether to come in (Luke 15:22–32).
sections.refs: Luke 14:15–24; Luke 15:22–32; Isaiah 25:6–9; Matthew 8:11; Matthew 22:1–14; Luke 13:28–29; Revelation 19:9

sections.h: Luke 14: whom to invite
sections.b: Jesus tells the leading Pharisee who invited him not to invite friends, family or rich neighbors who will invite him back, but the poor, crippled, lame and blind, "since they have no way to pay you back," and to look for repayment from God at the resurrection of the righteous (Luke 14:12–14). In a world where dinners were exchanges of favors and signs of rank, this turned hospitality from investment into gift. The same chapter warns guests against taking the top places (Luke 14:7–11), and the parable of the great supper shows a host who opens his house to those who can give nothing back (Luke 14:21–23).

sections.h: Luke 17: "the kingdom of God is among you"
sections.b: Asked by Pharisees when the kingdom of God was coming, Jesus answered that it does not come in a way that can be watched for, and that "the kingdom of God is among you" (Luke 17:20–21). The Greek ἐντὸς ὑμῶν can mean "within you" (KJV), the inner kingdom of many church fathers and of Tolstoy's book; "among you," present in Jesus and his deeds (Luke 11:20), the view of most modern scholars; or "within your reach." Luke then speaks of a future day when the Son of Man comes like lightning (Luke 17:24), so that the kingdom is both present and still to come. Luke 16:16 adds that the kingdom has been announced since John.

sections.h: Luke 17: the Samaritan who gave thanks
sections.b: Between Samaria and Galilee ten men with skin disease call to Jesus for mercy, and he sends them to the priests; on the way they are made clean. Only one turns back to give glory to God and thank Jesus, and "The man was a Samaritan" (Luke 17:16). Jesus calls him "this foreigner" (ἀλλογενής), the word carved on the temple's warning notices that barred non-Jews from its inner courts, and tells him, "Your faith has saved you" (Luke 17:18–19). With the Samaritan of Luke 10:33, he shows the outsider as the model, and prepares for the mission to Samaria in Acts 8. The scene recalls the foreigner Naaman, who returned to Elisha to give thanks (2 Kings 5:15; Luke 4:27).

sections.h: Luke 17: ten men sent to the priests
sections.b: Ten men with skin disease "kept their distance," as the Law required (Leviticus 13:45–46), and called to Jesus for mercy. He told them to go and let the priests see them, the inspection that the Law of cleansing required before a person could return to the community (Leviticus 14:1–32); they were made clean on the way, before they could see any change, as Naaman was healed only after he went and washed (2 Kings 5:10–14). For the Samaritan among them, "the priests" would have meant the Samaritan priesthood at Mount Gerizim.

sections.h: Luke 17: the days of the Son of Man
sections.b: Jesus tells his disciples that they will long to see "one of the days of the Son of Man" and will not; that the Son of Man will be like lightning that lights the whole sky "in his day"; but that first he "has to suffer much and be thrown out by this generation" (Luke 17:22–25). Luke places this saying about the cross in the middle of the teaching on the end: the Son of Man of Daniel 7 comes in glory only by way of rejection, as Psalm 118:22 foretold. His day will be "unveiled" suddenly, like the flood in Noah's time and the fire in Lot's (Luke 17:26–30).

sections.h: Luke 17: a sudden day without signs
sections.b: Luke separates two kinds of teaching about the future. In Luke 21 Jesus speaks of Jerusalem's destruction, with warning signs. In Luke 17 he speaks of the day of the Son of Man, which comes with no signs to calculate: "The kingdom of God does not come so that people can watch closely for it" (Luke 17:20). It will be sudden as lightning, and it will find people eating, drinking, buying and building, as in the days of Noah and Lot (Luke 17:24–30). On that day no one should turn back for possessions; "Remember Lot's wife!" (Luke 17:31–32). One will be taken along and the other left behind (Luke 17:34–35).

sections.h: Luke 17: "one will be taken along"
sections.b: Luke has the sayings about two in one bed and two women at the mill, "one will be taken along, and the other will be left behind" (Luke 17:34–35). Many Dispensationalists read the one "taken" as a believer caught up to Christ. Others point out that Luke's own examples, Noah and Lot, were taken out of danger while the rest were destroyed, which supports reading "taken" as rescue at Christ's coming but not a separate rapture; still others read "taken" as swept away in judgment, since the disciples' question "Where, Lord?" is answered with vultures gathering at a body (Luke 17:37). Luke 17:36 ("two in the field") is not in the oldest manuscripts.

sections.h: Luke 16: the Law still stands
sections.b: "The Law and the Prophets lasted until John. Since then the good news of the kingdom of God is being told" (Luke 16:16). Yet Luke at once adds that heaven and earth could pass away more easily than "one tiny hook of a letter could fall from the Law" (Luke 16:17), and gives Jesus' teaching on divorce, stricter than the Law's permission (Luke 16:18). In the parable that follows, Abraham sends the rich man's brothers to "Moses and the Prophets" as all they need (Luke 16:29–31). Jacob Jervell argued that Luke, more than any other Gospel writer, shows Jesus and the early believers as faithful to the Law. In Luke 17:14 Jesus sends ten healed men to the priests, as Leviticus 14 required.

sections.h: Luke 16:18: divorce without an exception
sections.b: Luke has a single verse on divorce, set between sayings about the Law and the parable of the rich man: "Everyone who divorces his wife and marries someone else commits adultery. And the man who marries a woman divorced from her husband commits adultery" (Luke 16:18). Like Mark 10:11–12, it has no exception; Matthew adds "except for sexual sin" (Matthew 5:32; 19:9). Luke speaks only of men, the ones who could give a divorce under Jewish law, and its place after Luke 16:17 shows Jesus' teaching as stricter than the Law's permission, not looser.
sections.refs: Luke 16:18; Mark 10:2–12; Matthew 5:31–32; Matthew 19:3–12; Deuteronomy 24:1–4; 1 Corinthians 7:10–11

sections.h: Luke 17: "Remember Lot's wife!"
sections.b: Only Luke adds Lot to Noah as an example of the coming day: in Sodom people ate, drank, bought, sold, planted and built, and on the day Lot went out, fire and sulfur rained from heaven (Luke 17:28–29). Then Jesus gives his shortest saying: "Remember Lot's wife!" (Luke 17:32). She left the city but looked back and became a pillar of salt (Genesis 19:26); on the day of the Son of Man, disciples must not turn back for their possessions. The Wisdom of Solomon calls the pillar a monument to an unbelieving soul (Wisdom of Solomon 10:7), and Josephus says he saw it (Antiquities 1.203).
sections.refs: Luke 17:28–33; Genesis 19:15–29; Wisdom of Solomon 10:6–7; 2 Peter 2:6–9

sections.h: Luke 17: the days of Noah
sections.b: "What happened in Noah's days will happen again in the days of the Son of Man" (Luke 17:26). People were eating and drinking and marrying "right up to the day Noah went into the ark. Then the flood came and wiped them all out" (Luke 17:27). The sin Jesus names is not violence but ordinary life lived without thought of God. Luke pairs Noah with Lot, as the Wisdom of Solomon and 2 Peter do.
sections.refs: Luke 17:26–27; Genesis 6:5–7:23; Matthew 24:37–39; 2 Peter 2:5; Wisdom of Solomon 10:4

sections.h: Luke 14–17: at table, grumbling, and asking about the kingdom
sections.b: In these chapters Jesus dines at the house of a leading Pharisee on the Sabbath and debates healing with the lawyers and Pharisees there (Luke 14:1–6); Pharisees and scribes grumble at his meals with sinners, and he answers with the three parables of the lost (Luke 15:1–2); Pharisees "fond of money" sneer at his teaching on wealth (Luke 16:14); and Pharisees ask him when the kingdom of God is coming (Luke 17:20). Luke's portrait is mixed: the Pharisees host Jesus and argue with him as Jewish teachers did, but Luke also charges them with love of money, a stock accusation that Josephus' description of the Pharisees' simple life does not support (Antiquities 18.12).

sections.h: Luke 14: counting the cost
sections.b: When large crowds followed Jesus, he turned and set out the cost: whoever does not "hate" father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters, and even his own life, cannot be his disciple, and the same for anyone who does not carry his own cross and come behind him (Luke 14:25–27). "Hate" is a Hebrew way of saying "put second"; Matthew has "loves over me" (Matthew 10:37). Twin parables, a man building a tower and a king going to war, tell people to count the cost first (Luke 14:28–32), and the section ends, "none of you can be a disciple of mine if he does not say goodbye to all his possessions" (Luke 14:33). Luke 17:7–10 adds that a disciple who has done everything has only done his duty.

sections.h: Luke 14: "Compel them to come in" (Latin compelle intrare)
sections.b: In the parable of the great supper the master tells his slave to go out to the roads and hedgerows "and make them come in" (Luke 14:23), urgent hospitality to strangers who would politely refuse. In its Latin form, compelle intrare, the verse became Augustine's proof-text for imperial laws forcing the Donatists back into the Catholic Church (Letters 93 and 185), and later writers used it to justify the persecution of heretics. Pierre Bayle's Philosophical Commentary (1686) argued that a reading of Scripture that commands cruelty must be false. All the major churches now reject the use of force in matters of faith; the history is told on the Luke 14 chapter page.

sections.h: Luke 14: a son or an ox in a well
sections.b: At a Sabbath meal in a leading Pharisee's house, Jesus asks the lawyers and Pharisees whether it is allowed to heal on the Sabbath, heals a man swollen with dropsy, and asks which of them would not haul a son or an ox out of a well at once, even on the Sabbath (Luke 14:1–6). Jewish groups differed: the Damascus Document forbids lifting an animal out of a pit on the Sabbath, while later rabbis allowed indirect help and held that saving life overrides the Sabbath (Mishnah Yoma 8:6). It is Luke's fourth Sabbath healing.
sections.refs: Luke 14:1–6; Luke 6:6–11; Luke 13:10–17; Exodus 20:8–11; Deuteronomy 22:4; Matthew 12:11–12

sections.h: Luke 15 and 17: slaves and sons
sections.b: Two passages in Luke use slavery as a picture. The elder son in the parable of the two sons says, "I have worked like a slave for you," though he is a son and heir (Luke 15:29–31), while the younger son hopes only to be a hired man (Luke 15:19). In Luke 17:7–10 Jesus takes for granted a small farmer with one slave who plows by day and serves supper at night, and draws the lesson that disciples who have done everything are "useless slaves" who have only done their duty. The parable uses the institution without approving it, and Luke has already pictured a master who serves his own slaves (Luke 12:37).

sections.h: Luke 16–17: justifying yourself, and "useless slaves"
sections.b: Jesus tells Pharisees who sneered at him, "You justify yourselves in people's eyes, but God knows your hearts" (Luke 16:15). In Luke 17:10 he tells the apostles that when they have done all they were ordered, they should say, "We are useless slaves. What we were bound to do, we have done." The verse was cited in the Reformation against works of supererogation and human merit (Thirty-Nine Articles 14; Westminster Confession 16.5), while Catholic teaching holds that the merits of the justified are real and are God's own gifts (Council of Trent, session 6). See the card on Luke 17.

sections.h: Luke 16: the manager's discounts
sections.b: The manager in Luke 16:1–8 calls in his master's debtors and has them rewrite their bills, a hundred baths of olive oil reduced to fifty, a hundred cors of wheat to eighty. One reading, argued by J. D. M. Derrett, is that the bills included interest forbidden by the Law (Deuteronomy 23:19; Exodus 22:25), hidden in the amount owed, so the manager made his master righteous by the Law; the larger cut on oil fits the higher rates charged on oil. Others think he cut his own commission, or simply cheated his master again.

sections.h: Luke 16: friends who welcome you into the everlasting tents
sections.b: "Make yourselves friends out of the wealth of dishonesty, so that when it runs out, they will take you into the everlasting tents" (Luke 16:9). Many readers take the "friends" to be the poor, whom gifts of money make into friends who will welcome the giver in the age to come, an idea close to Tobit's teaching that alms rescue from death (Tobit 4:10). The parable of the rich man and Lazarus shows the opposite: the poor man at the gate is ignored, and the rich man finds no welcome (Luke 16:19–26).

sections.h: Luke 14 and 16: repaid at the resurrection, and one who rises from the dead
sections.b: Jesus tells a Pharisee host that those who invite the poor "will be paid back at the resurrection of the righteous" (Luke 14:14), a hope Pharisees shared against the Sadducees (Acts 23:8). The parable of the rich man and Lazarus ends with Abraham's words that those who do not listen to Moses and the Prophets will not be persuaded "even if someone rises from the dead" (Luke 16:31), which Christian readers have long heard as pointing to Jesus' own resurrection and to Lazarus of Bethany (John 11; 12:10).
sections.refs: Luke 14:14; Luke 16:31; Daniel 12:2; Acts 24:15; John 11:43–53; John 12:9–11

sections.h: Luke 16: Abraham's embrace
sections.b: In the parable of the rich man and Lazarus, angels carry the poor man to "Abraham's embrace," the place of honor next to the host at the feast of the righteous dead (Luke 16:22). The rich man calls Abraham "Father," and Abraham calls him "My child," yet the family tie cannot cross the great gulf (Luke 16:24–26), as John the Baptist warned against relying on Abraham as father (Luke 3:8). Abraham himself sends the rich man's brothers to Moses and the Prophets (Luke 16:29).
sections.refs: Luke 16:22–31; Luke 3:8; Luke 13:16, 28; Luke 19:9; John 8:39; 4 Maccabees 13:17

sections.h: Luke 15: the elder son read as "the Jews"
sections.b: Some church fathers read the two sons of Luke 15 as the Gentiles (the younger, welcomed) and the Jews (the elder, refusing to come in); Jerome discusses this reading in his Letter 21. The reading was easy to turn into contempt. Luke's own frame is a debate within Israel, between Jesus and Pharisees and scribes who object to his meals with Jewish "tax collectors and sinners" (Luke 15:1–2), and the father's last words to the elder son are tender: "My child, you are with me all the time, and all I have belongs to you" (Luke 15:31). Amy-Jill Levine and others have asked Christian readers to hear the parable without making the elder son a figure for the Jewish people.

sections.h: Luke 17: faith like a mustard seed, and faith that saves
sections.b: The apostles ask, "Give us more faith!", after being told to forgive without limit. Jesus answers that faith the size of a mustard seed could tell a mulberry tree to be uprooted and planted in the sea (Luke 17:5–6): the question is not how much faith, but faith in God at all. In the same chapter, one of ten men cleansed of skin disease turns back to give thanks, and Jesus tells him, "Your faith has saved you" (Luke 17:19), with the verb that means both "heal" and "save."
sections.refs: Luke 17:5–6; Luke 17:19; Matthew 17:20; Mark 11:22–23; Luke 7:50; Luke 8:48; Luke 18:42
